projectDetail:
A mobile arcade game where you drive an armored wrecker down a highway and smash whatever is in front of you. Wrecks pay cash, cash buys upgrades, and a stronger truck gets further down the road before it dies. One thumb, short runs, built portrait for phones.

Traffic is not scenery. Every vehicle has a weight class, so a bike folds on contact while an armored van shrugs off a bad hit, and a car you launch can shunt the next one into a chain. The drivers react as well. Some spin out, some turn on you, some try to get away.
myContribution:
1. Built the truck handling: steering that turns nose-first with weight behind it, body roll off sideways acceleration, wheel motion, and the bob and pitch that sell the suspension.
2. Built the wrecking model. Every vehicle carries a weight class and its own HP, hits are aimed like a paddle, and a launched wreck can shunt the next vehicle along.
3. Wrote the chain rules so longer and more varied chains pay bonus cash, with weight respected: a light wreck chips a heavy vehicle instead of deleting it.
4. Built reactive traffic. Rams spin cars out, some drivers turn aggressive, some flee, and the mix changes section by section down the road.
5. Built the Garage: Engine, Ram and Body at five tiers each, driven from the per-vehicle level tables in the design doc.
6. Built the World Tour map select with per-map unlocks, and the map data that drives each run's zones, traffic, roadside and gates.
7. Moved the chase camera onto Cinemachine and gave it lean through turns to match the prototype framing.
8. Built the UI in UI Toolkit: HUD, speedometer, pause and results screens, map cards, and the run intro with its countdown and engine hold.
9. Set up Addressables so each map's art loads on demand instead of shipping every environment in the build.
10. Wired the plumbing underneath: save data, object pooling, scene loading, input actions with gamepad and keyboard alongside drag steering, and Android haptics.

additionalDetails.title: Weight Classes, and What Actually Breaks
additionalDetails.description: The first pass wrecked every vehicle in one hit, which made the whole road feel like paper and left nothing to upgrade toward. Weight class now decides. Light traffic always goes down in one. Everything heavier loses HP per hit, side hits wear it down, and armored vehicles carry a shield on top. The rule that pulled it together is that a lighter wreck can only chip a heavier vehicle, never delete it, which is what makes a Ram upgrade something you feel rather than read. Bikes needed their own Super Light class once the rest settled.

additionalDetails.title: Chains
additionalDetails.description: Hits are aimed rather than absorbed. Where you catch a vehicle decides which way it launches, closer to a paddle than a bumper, and a launched wreck can take the next vehicle with it. Longer and more varied chains pay bonus cash, so the skill ceiling is lining up a hit that clears three cars instead of one. The weight rules keep it honest, otherwise one lucky bike would clear a lane of trucks.

additionalDetails.title: Maps Loaded On Demand
additionalDetails.description: World Tour splits each map into sections, and a section owns its zones, traffic mix, roadside dressing and gates, so the same drive changes character as you move through it. Art is the expensive part on mobile, so each map's environment loads through Addressables rather than sitting in the build. The first content build is done and the maps drive the game scene from their own data, which means a new location is a data and art job rather than a code one.

projectDetail:
A Roblox heist game. Your crew robs a shop, takes whatever is worth money and gets out before the police arrive. Cash rides in a bag on your back and only counts once it reaches the escape van.

Heat is the clock. It climbs on its own and spikes when someone spots you, calls it in, or you start shooting. When the timer runs out the police show up, and how many of them depends on how much Heat you made. Everyone in the building is a live NPC, so a quiet job and a loud one play nothing alike.
myContribution:
1. Built the NPC system. Agents with behaviours swapped at runtime, and character types kept as shared config instead of subclasses.
2. Wrote the perception layer: line-of-sight checks, witness detection, and the weighted roll that decides whether someone cowers, runs or calls the police.
3. Built the police. Unit roster, chase behaviour with cover and strafing, and waves sized by the Heat earned and the number of players.
4. Replaced Roblox pathfinding with a raycast-built nav grid and A*. Cover positions come off the same grid.
5. Built the Area of Control: how much of the room the crew holds, and whether an NPC gets intimidated instead of shot.
6. Built player health, knockdowns, timed co-op revives, and the loot you drop when you go down.
7. Built loot and breakables, including props that drop one to three random items per round, plus carry weight.
8. Built the vault, the door systems and the in-game tutorial.
9. Owned the live-service side: lobby, daily rewards, leaderboards, equipment and stat upgrades, monetization and anti-cheat.
10. Tuned difficulty so NPC count, toughness, payout and keycards scale with crew size.
11. Built the debug tooling the team tests with, and wrote the system docs.
engine: Roblox Studio, Luau (Rojo, Knit, Roact, Rodux)

additionalDetails.title: Dropping Roblox's Pathfinder
additionalDetails.description: NPCs kept walking into walls and shelving. The real cause was that the engine's navmesh disagreed with what a raycast actually hits: mesh walls skipped by collision fidelity, shelf tops counted as floor, and one global agent radius trying to serve both a shop aisle and a security guard. I rebuilt navigation on a grid rasterised from raycasts and searched it with eight-way A*, so the map cannot disagree with physics. Clearance became per character type, asked for at search time. Making the search synchronous deleted the request queue, the straight-line fallback and the retry counters, and the movement agent lost two thirds of its code. The same grid later became where police look for cover.

additionalDetails.title: Heat
additionalDetails.description: A plain countdown makes every round feel the same, so Heat does two jobs. It climbs on its own, which gives the round a horizon, and it jumps when the crew is spotted, reported or shooting. Players see a five-star bar with no number, so they read pressure instead of doing arithmetic. When the timer ends the round escalates rather than stopping: the police get a budget sized by the Heat earned and spend it on waves of officers, SWAT and military. A quiet crew meets a few officers. A loud one gets besieged.

additionalDetails.title: NPCs You Can Talk Down
additionalDetails.description: Every customer, clerk and guard is a live agent rather than a prop, which had to stay cheap with a building full of them. One agent class owns a model and its health, behaviours are separate objects swapped at runtime, and archetypes are read-only tables every NPC of that type points at. Police are the only subclass. Area of Control is what makes a quiet run possible: inside it an NPC can be intimidated into compliance, outside it they are free to run for an alarm.

projectDetail:
A Roblox game about cleaning up after the heist instead of pulling it off. Your crew lands in a crime scene on a timer: scrub the blood, grind up the evidence and the bodies, put moved furniture back where it was, hack the panels that open locked rooms and the vault, and drag the hostages out.

On top of that sits a full live-service loop. Levels unlock maps and difficulties, cash and XP feed equipment and stat upgrades, and seasonal events such as Clown, Ghost and Glitch bring their own maps and objectives.
myContribution:
1. Built the grab, carry and drop system that the whole game runs on, including a client-side grab for responsiveness, a ghost preview, and PC, mobile and gamepad support.
2. Built the grinder that turns collected evidence into payout.
3. Built the door system: hacking panels spawned at random each run, multi-panel vault doors, and placement rules that keep every run solvable.
4. Built the hostage objective end to end, from spawning and rope-constrained dragging through to the delivery zone.
5. Built the rearrange-object and generator objectives with their spawners and task templates.
6. Owned the mission flow. Refactored the mission service, split out its logic, added the exit handler and built the animated summary screen.
7. Owned the lobby: host panel, map and difficulty selection with level gating, teleport flow and two versions of the party system.
8. Built the equipment system with its shop, tier previews and upgrade progression, plus the stat upgrade panels.
9. Built the monetization layer. Gamepasses, dev products, packs, limited starter and VIP offers, and one shared product registry so every storefront grants through the same path.
10. Built the retention systems: seven-day daily rewards with offline grants, daily tasks, free chests, the spin wheel and referrals.
11. Built the Clown event and the seasonal event maps with their own objectives.
12. Wrote the input system with rebindable actions and console support, plus the shared UI pieces used across the front end.
13. Added analytics and funnel events for the lobby, tutorial, map selection and failed interactions.
engine: Roblox Studio, Luau (Rojo, Knit, Roact, Rodux)

additionalDetails.title: Randomised Door Panels
additionalDetails.description: Locked rooms and the vault open by hacking panels scattered at mission start instead of placed by hand, so no two runs are the same. Five spawn each round and the vault needs two of them. The hard part was the rules that keep it solvable: a panel can never sit locked inside the room it opens, only so many may sit inside locked rooms at all, and each locked room holds at most one. Spawn points carry their room, whether it is locked, and how near a door they are. Distance is a preference. Solvability is not.

additionalDetails.title: Grabbing Things Over the Network
additionalDetails.description: Picking things up is the main verb of the game, so it had to feel instant while the server stayed in charge. The grab runs locally for feedback and reconciles with a server service that owns the real state. Most of the work went into physical edge cases: grab offsets on odd-shaped meshes, bodies resting upright against a wall, objects re-entering a grab mid-grind, and geometry you could trigger through a wall. Carry capacity later became something players could buy, on top of the same system.

additionalDetails.title: An Economy That Survives Disconnects
additionalDetails.description: The game sells gamepasses, dev products, limited offers and packs across several storefronts that all had to agree with each other, so purchases grant through one shared product registry rather than each panel rolling its own. Most of the effort went into the paths players never see. Entitlements get reconciled when a session dies mid-transaction, offers and reward streaks run on server time rather than the device clock, and rewards earned offline land on the next login.

projectDetail: "Block Tiles Earn Cyrpto" is a blockchain-integrated game inspired by classic block-stacking gameplay. Players are rewarded with virtual currency based on the number of lines they clear during gameplay. Once users accumulate enough currency, they can request real-world payouts directly to their Binance or Coinbase account. This system incentivizes skillful play while integrating a real-money reward mechanism.
myContribution:
1. Implemented multiple authentication options including Email, Facebook, Google, and Guest login.
2. Integrated PlayFab backend for account management, economy, and data handling.
3. Added AdMob monetization including Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded, and App Open Ads.
4. Developed Binance withdrawal functionality for crypto payouts.
5. Strengthened security to prevent exploits and cheating behaviors.
6. Provided live support to players with login and account-related issues.
7. Diagnosed and resolved gameplay and system bugs across devices.

additionalDetails.title: Reward System & Payout Mechanism
additionalDetails.description: One of the key challenges was implementing a reward structure that balanced engaging gameplay with real-world payouts. Users were awarded virtual currency upon completing levels based on difficulty. Once they reached the withdrawal threshold, they could request payment to their Binance or Coinbase accounts by submitting their email. Ensuring this system was seamless, secure, and abuse-proof required thoughtful design and ongoing refinement.

additionalDetails.title: Exploits & Fair Play
additionalDetails.description: As the game involved real monetary value, preventing unfair advantages was critical. One notable exploit involved users manipulating their device's local time to bypass the withdrawal cooldown period. To counter this, we integrated PlayFab's trusted server time to validate all withdrawal timing and enforce cooldowns reliably. Users attempting to bypass this mechanism were automatically flagged and temporarily banned. Ongoing monitoring and backend-side validation helped maintain a fair and cheat-free environment.

projectDetail: "Minesweeper Earn Crypto" is a blockchain-integrated casual game inspired by the classic Minesweeper gameplay. Players could choose from three difficulty levels — Easy, Medium, and Hard — and were awarded virtual currency upon successfully clearing each round. The reward amount varied depending on the selected difficulty. Once players accumulated enough virtual currency, they could initiate a withdrawal by providing their Binance or Coinbase email address, allowing them to receive crypto payouts directly to their exchange wallets. The game blended nostalgic gameplay with real-world incentives, encouraging both strategy and engagement.

projectDetail: A custom inventory and order management app designed to streamline operations across two family-run businesses — a tiles and sanitary dealership, and a wall paint store. The system adapts to the unique workflows and measurement units of each showroom, ensuring accurate stock, order, and role-based access management.
myContribution:
1. Developed custom login with access-level-based dashboards.
2. Implemented dual-unit product ordering (sft/carton vs. pieces).
3. Integrated Google Sheets import for bulk stock entry.
4. Developed dynamic UI to separate tiles and paint showroom workflows.
5. Handled inventory, order, and user account management.

additionalDetails.title: Complex Unit Handling
additionalDetails.description: Each product followed a different measurement standard — such as square feet, cartons, pieces, grams, or liters. The system had to intelligently identify and adapt to each type for accurate stock tracking and billing.

additionalDetails.title: PDF Invoice Generation Without Unity SDK
additionalDetails.description: I used Unity 3D to develop my app because I am a game developer and not familiar with other app frameworks. Since there is no PDF generator SDK in Unity, I had to use a .NET PDF library to create invoice PDF files directly from the Unity app.

additionalDetails.title: High-Stakes Validation Challenges
additionalDetails.description: Accurate calculations were critical. A small logic or validation issue could lead to discrepancies in billing, risking business credibility. Rapid debugging and issue resolution were essential to maintain trust with customers.
